explanations.explanation: Anger it is, friend. The writer opens with “How the Lord has covered the Daughter of Zion with the cloud of His anger!” That exclamation point is doing real work. This poem isn't tiptoeing in, and from line one you know what the weather is.

Glory is in this verse, but it's in the next line, and it's what gets thrown down. The writer says the Lord “has cast the glory of Israel from heaven to earth.” The cloud itself is made of His anger. I've grabbed the wrong jar lid off the shelf plenty of times, so I get it.

Mercy doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The writer says the cloud is the cloud of His anger, and then says the glory of Israel has been cast from heaven to earth. The poem starts heavy and doesn't soften it. Hold on, because the writer keeps going.

That's the phrase, friend. The verse begins, “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” The writer puts it right at the front, so you can't miss it. This is a poem of grief, and the writer says the loss plainly.

Regret isn't in this verse. The writer says the opposite: “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” Pity is the very thing the writer says is missing. It's a hard line, and the poem doesn't dress it up.

The writer never says anything about speed here. The verse says “Without pity the Lord has swallowed up all the dwellings of Jacob.” The word that matters is pity, and it's missing. Easy to guess a detail the text doesn't give, friend.

The first half is true, but the second half flips it. The writer says the Lord has “cut off every horn of Israel” and has “…withdrawn His right hand at the approach of the enemy.” So His right hand is pulled back, not held out to defend. Watch for a true start that carries a false ending.

Right, and the catch is in the second half. The writer says the Lord has “…withdrawn His right hand at the approach of the enemy.” So He holds back His hand instead of holding it out for Israel. The first half, cutting off every horn of Israel, is exactly what the verse says.

Yes, the bow. The writer says, “He has bent His bow like an enemy; His right hand is positioned.” That's a picture of someone aimed and ready. The poem uses "like an enemy" to describe the scene, so I'll leave it right there.

A sword does show up in this poem, but not here. Later the writer says young men and maidens have fallen by the sword (Lamentations 2:21). In this verse the weapon is a bow: “He has bent His bow like an enemy.” Right chapter, wrong verse, friend.

There's no spear anywhere in this passage, friend. The verse says, “He has bent His bow like an enemy; His right hand is positioned.” The weapon in the picture is a bow. I'd have guessed a spear too, to be honest, but the text has other plans.

True. The Lord has swallowed up Israel and all her palaces, and destroyed her strongholds. Then the writer says He “has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.” This is the verse where the grief piles up. I think the writer wants you to feel the weight of it.

It's true, friend. The writer says the Lord has swallowed up Israel and all her palaces and destroyed her strongholds. Then the verse ends, “He has multiplied mourning and lamentation for the Daughter of Judah.” It sounds like a lot to say about one city, but that's what the text says.

That's the one. The writer says, “The LORD has made Zion forget her appointed feasts and Sabbaths.” Those were the special days that set the rhythm of her year. In the same verse, the Lord despises both king and priest.

Enemies come up in this poem, but their names don't. What Zion is made to forget is “her appointed feasts and Sabbaths.” The writer says it right there in verse 6. I'd say forgetting the Sabbaths is a heavy loss.

Prophets get their own line later, friend. In verse 9 they find no vision from the LORD. What Zion is made to forget in verse 6 is “her appointed feasts and Sabbaths.” It's easy to mix them up when the poem keeps stacking losses.

The writer says it differently. In His fierce anger the Lord “has despised both king and priest.” So the priest isn't spared, and both of them are named in the same breath. It's one word, "both," that makes the difference.
Right. The writer says the Lord, in His fierce anger, “has despised both king and priest.” The priest isn't left out, and both are named together. That one little word "both" carries the whole verse.

explanations.answer: In the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the place. The writer says, “They have raised a shout in the house of the LORD as on the day of an appointed feast.” The enemy is shouting right inside the house of the LORD. I think that's why this line stings so much.

The shout is closer than that, friend. The writer says it is raised “in the house of the LORD as on the day of an appointed feast.” The gates come up in verse 9, where they've sunk into the ground. This verse is about the house itself.

The ramparts have a different job in this poem. In verse 8, the writer says the ramparts and walls lament. The shout in verse 7 is raised “in the house of the LORD as on the day of an appointed feast.” A lot of stone in this chapter, I know.

True. The gates have sunk into the ground, the king and princes are exiled among the nations, and the writer says “the law is no more.” That's a lot of things going missing in one verse. Even the prophets are mentioned right after.

It's true, friend. The verse says her gates have sunk into the ground, her king and princes are exiled among the nations, and “the law is no more.” That last part is in the text, word for word. The poem puts it right alongside the other losses.
Yes. The writer says, “even her prophets find no vision from the LORD.” A prophet without a vision has nothing to pass along. It's quiet in the city, and the poem tells you why.

That's not what the verse says. It says her prophets “find no vision from the LORD.” Nothing is given to them, so there's nothing to pass along. A message of peace would be welcome, but the text says no vision.

No song is mentioned here, friend. The verse says even her prophets “find no vision from the LORD.” The poem is heavy in this stretch and doesn't hand out a new song. Hold tight, because the next stop moves on.

Faint is the word. The writer says his heart is poured out in grief because “children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” This is the heart of why he's weeping. I think this is where the poem gets personal.

Playing in the streets would be a happy picture, and that's not this one. The writer grieves because “children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” The word is faint, friend. It's a heavy verse and the poem says it plainly.

Hiding isn't in this verse. The writer says his heart is poured out in grief because “children and infants faint in the streets of the city.” They're out in the open, and they faint. It's hard to read, and I'm not going to joke about it.

explanations.answer: Where is the grain and wine
explanations.explanation: Yes. The children cry out to their mothers, “Where is the grain and wine?” The writer says it as they faint like the wounded in the streets. I think this verse hurts, and it's okay to feel that.

explanations.answer: When will our fathers come home
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. What the children cry to their mothers is “Where is the grain and wine?” It's a cry for something to eat and drink. I think that's what makes it so heavy.

explanations.answer: Where did all the soldiers go
explanations.explanation: Soldiers aren't part of this cry. The children say to their mothers, “Where is the grain and wine?” They're asking for food and drink. It's a heavy verse, and the poem lets it stand.

The poem says the opposite. The writer tells her, “your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?” So it's deep, and the writer doesn't promise a quick fix. He's searching for words to console her, and it's not coming easily.
Right. The writer says, “your wound is as deep as the sea. Who can ever heal you?” Nothing about it is small. He's looking for a way to console her, and even he can't find the words.
That's what the writer says. “The visions of your prophets were empty and deceptive.” He says the burdens they envisioned were “empty and misleading,” too. Same word twice, so I think he means it.
The text doesn't say that, friend. The writer says the visions of her prophets “were empty and deceptive.” Nothing about them coming true. He's pointing at what they left unsaid.

explanations.answer: They were too hard to understand
explanations.explanation: The problem isn't that they were confusing. The writer says the visions “were empty and deceptive,” and the burdens they envisioned were “empty and misleading.” Empty and misleading is a different problem than hard to follow. It was the visions themselves that let her down.

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says the prophets “did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity.” So they didn't expose it, and the captivity came. That's what makes their visions empty.

Right. The writer says her prophets “did not expose your guilt to ward off your captivity.” They didn't expose her guilt, and the captivity wasn't warded off. It's one of the sharpest lines in the poem.

explanations.answer: Clap their hands at her in scorn
explanations.explanation: That's it. The writer says, “All who pass by clap their hands at you in scorn.” They hiss and shake their heads, too. It's a lot of noise for a city in ruins, and none of it is kind.

That one belongs to someone else. The elders of the Daughter of Zion “have thrown dust on their heads” back in verse 10. The passersby in verse 15 “clap their hands at you in scorn.” It's a different crowd with a very different mood.

explanations.answer: Bow their heads to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's the young women of Jerusalem in verse 10, friend. They “have bowed their heads to the ground.” The passersby in verse 15 do something else: they “clap their hands at you in scorn.” They're grieving in one verse and scorning in the other.
Yes. They say, “This is the day for which we have waited. We have lived to see it!” So they were expecting it, and they're glad it came. That's a hard thing to hear from enemies.
Surprise isn't what they say. Zion's enemies say, “This is the day for which we have waited.” They'd been waiting for it. That's the opposite of caught off guard.
No regret in their words, friend. They say, “We have swallowed her up. This is the day for which we have waited. We have lived to see it!” They sound pleased, and the poem doesn't soften that.

True. The writer says, “The LORD has done what He planned; He has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old.” So the decree goes back to days of old. The poem says it plainly and doesn't add why.

It's true, friend. The verse says the LORD “has accomplished His decree, which He ordained in days of old.” That phrase is right there in the text. It's worth reading slow, and the poem doesn't hurry past it.
That's it. The poem says to let your tears run down like a river “day and night.” Then it adds, “Give yourself no relief, and your eyes no rest.” It's a call to keep crying out, not to hold it in.
The poem doesn't set an end time like that. It says to let your tears run down like a river “day and night.” That covers both halves of the clock. No sunrise cutoff in this verse, friend.
There's no number of days in this verse. The poem says to let your tears run down like a river “day and night.” It doesn't count them out. It just says to give yourself no relief.

Children, yes. The poem says to lift up your hands to Him “for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.” That's who the prayer is for. I think it's a prayer you can feel.

Soldiers aren't in this verse. The poem says to lift up your hands to Him “for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.” It's children who are fainting from hunger. That's who the prayer is for.

The elders are in verse 10, friend, where they sit on the ground in silence. In verse 19, the hands are lifted up “for the lives of your children who are fainting from hunger on the corner of every street.” Different verse, different people.

explanations.answer: Whom have You ever treated like this
explanations.explanation: That's the question. The prayer says, “Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?” It's the poem speaking straight to the LORD. It asks Him to look first, and then it asks.

explanations.answer: How long will this go on
explanations.explanation: That's a fair question, but it isn't in this verse. The prayer says, “Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?” It asks Him to look and consider first. Then comes the question about whom He has treated this way.

explanations.answer: When will You rebuild our walls
explanations.explanation: No rebuilding is asked for in this verse, friend. The prayer says, “Look, O LORD, and consider: Whom have You ever treated like this?” It's a cry to be seen. The poem doesn't add a request about walls.

True. The prayer asks, “Should women eat their offspring, the infants they have nurtured?” Then it asks, “Should priests and prophets be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord?” These are two very heavy questions. I think the poem is laying them before God on purpose.

It's true, friend. Both questions are right there in verse 20. The prayer asks if women should eat their offspring, the infants they have nurtured, and if priests and prophets should be killed in the sanctuary of the Lord. They're hard to read, and the poem doesn't hide them.

The second half is where it turns. The writer says, “In the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped or survived.” So not a few, but no one. The first half, terrors summoned on every side, is in the text.
Right. The writer says, “In the day of the LORD’s anger no one escaped or survived.” So there isn't a few who made it out. The first part is true, since terrors were summoned on every side.
